tagline: River ports and abandoned channels trace a changing Mississippi landscape.
intro: The Lower Mississippi Historic Scenic Byway parallels the Mississippi for more than a hundred miles. The Federal Highway Administration lists a two-hour drive and presents the route in America’s Byways for its sites connected with antebellum America, the Civil War and its aftermath.

The river itself changed the journeys made here. In 1876, a flood cut off the bend beside Vicksburg, leaving the port on an oxbow lake and damaging its economy. The Army Corps of Engineers completed the Yazoo Diversion Canal in 1903, restoring water access after much passenger and freight traffic had shifted to rail.

From Vicksburg’s high bluff, US 61 heads south toward Port Gibson and Natchez. Windsor’s standing columns lie southwest of Port Gibson; farther south, Rodney occupies a former river landing northeast of Natchez. The southern excursion to Clark Creek leads west of Woodville into the Tunica Hills, where erosion has cut steep ravines beneath loess-covered ridges.

moments.title: Windsor Ruins
moments.text: Twenty-three Corinthian columns remain where Windsor mansion stood from 1861 until an 1890 fire. Enslaved African Americans worked alongside northern masons and New England carpenters to build it for cotton planter Smith Coffee Daniell II. The columns were brick under stucco, capped with ornate ironwork shipped from St. Louis down the Mississippi. Windsor survived the Civil War, when Union troops used it as a hospital. The later fire began when a guest’s cigarette or cigar ashes fell into carpenters’ debris. One surviving iron stairway was moved to Alcorn State University’s Oakland Memorial Chapel.
moments.notice: The surviving columns have fluted shafts and iron Corinthian capitals.

moments.title: Rodney
moments.text: Rodney’s former shipping channel became a swamp as the Mississippi shifted west. The port declined, the railroad ran through Fayette instead, and Rodney lost its incorporation in 1930. Its Presbyterian church preserves a different kind of evidence. In September 1863, Confederate cavalry captured men from USS Rattler attending a service; the ship then shelled the town. The hole in the church wall was retained during restoration, but the cannonball placed there is a replica. It sits above the balcony windows on the damaged façade. Recurrent flooding has left extensive damage to the town’s remaining buildings.

moments.title: Clark Creek Natural Area
moments.text: Clark Creek’s approximately 50 waterfalls belong to the dissected terrain of the Tunica Hills. Some drop as much as 30 feet. Erosion has cut steep ravines through layered sediments below ridges covered with loess, a wind-blown silt. The creek cuts through more than 400 feet of sediment. The forest mixes hardwoods and pines, including large beech and magnolia trees. Established in 1978 through public and private efforts, the natural area lies approximately 13 miles west of Woodville. Its improved trails include pea gravel and steep wooden stairs, with the sloping bluffs adding to the difficulty of the walk.
